items.title: Integration by parts is the product rule played backwards
items.claim: The product rule: d(uv)/dx = u'v + uv'. Rearrange: uv' = d(uv)/dx - u'v. Integrate: integral of uv' dx = uv - integral of u'v dx. The formula isn't a separate tool — it's the product rule, integrated.

options.text: Choose u as the type higher in 'ILATE' priority: Inverse trig, Logarithmic, Algebraic, Trigonometric, Exponential. These tend to become simpler when differentiated; choosing them as u makes u'v easier to integrate than the original

items.reveal_title: Integration by parts and clever choices
items.reveal:
Integration by parts: integral of u dv = uv - integral of v du.

The formula always works mathematically, but the resulting integral can be HARDER than the original if you choose u and dv poorly. The ILATE heuristic helps:
- I: Inverse trig (arctan, arcsin)
- L: Logarithmic (ln x)
- A: Algebraic (polynomials)
- T: Trigonometric (sin, cos)
- E: Exponential (e^x)

Choose u as the FIRST function appearing in this list. Choose dv as the LAST.

Why: logarithmic and inverse trig functions become algebraic when differentiated; polynomials become lower-degree polynomials. Exponentials and most trig functions stay similar under differentiation, so we'd rather integrate them.

Classical applications:
- integral of x e^x dx: u = x, dv = e^x dx. Result: x e^x - e^x + C.
- integral of x sin x dx: u = x, dv = sin x dx. Result: -x cos x + sin x + C.
- integral of ln x dx: u = ln x, dv = dx. Result: x ln x - x + C.
- integral of x^2 e^x dx: apply twice.

Tabular integration (D-I tabular method) systematises repeated applications.

The Frullani integral, Bessel functions, and many special-function identities come from clever integration by parts. It's not just a textbook drill; it's the algebraic shadow of one of the deepest theorems in calculus (the fundamental theorem applied to product structures).
items.why: Integration by parts is taught as a mechanical technique. It's the product rule running backwards — and the ILATE heuristic is empirical wisdom about which functions are easier to differentiate than integrate.

items.title: Two equal pours of wine and water never separate again
items.claim: Pour a cup of wine into a barrel of water. Stir. Now pour a cup of the mixture back into the wine. Compared to the original: is there more wine in the water-barrel, or more water in the wine-barrel?

options.text: More wine in water (because it was poured first)
More water in wine (because the second cup contained mixture, not pure water)
Equal — by conservation of volume, the amount of wine missing from the wine barrel exactly equals the amount of water now in the wine barrel
Cannot be determined without more information

items.reveal:
Both barrels started with their own volume (V wine and V water). After two exchanges of one cup each, the volumes are still V wine and V water (volume is conserved in each barrel).

Let's say the wine barrel now contains x amount of water and (V - x) wine. The wine barrel's contents totals V — so by mass balance, V - (V - x) = x amount of wine has LEFT the wine barrel. Where did it go? It is now in the water barrel.

So: water in wine barrel = x; wine in water barrel = x. Always equal — regardless of how messy the mixing was, or whether the cups were exact, or how much you stirred.

This is a classic riddle dating to mediaeval mathematics. People reach for arithmetic and get tangled in fractions. A two-line conservation argument settles it without computation.

Generalisation: for ANY pair of equal-volume transfers (cup A to barrel B, then equal-volume cup B' to barrel A), the impurity in each ends up equal. The riddle is independent of mixing details.

Lesson for problem-solving: pure-conservation arguments often resolve mixing problems faster than direct calculation. The same idea underlies many chemistry-stoichiometry problems and the 'rule of alligation' in pharmacy.
items.why: Mixing problems feel like they need detailed arithmetic. Conservation reasoning bypasses the arithmetic entirely — and is more reliable, because it's robust to the details you don't know.

items.title: 45 degrees is only optimal for a projectile in a vacuum
items.claim: Every physics textbook says the maximum range for a projectile is at launch angle 45 degrees. True in vacuum. In real air, the optimum angle is significantly less — and for some launches it's barely above 30 degrees.
items.prompt: Why does air change the optimum?

options.text: It doesn't — 45 degrees is always optimal
Air resistance reduces both horizontal velocity and vertical velocity, but the loss to drag is greater on long airborne paths; lowering the angle reduces flight time and total drag exposure
Gravity is different at high angles

items.reveal:
Vacuum case: range = (v^2 / g) * sin(2 * theta). Maximised at theta = 45 degrees.

With linear drag (low-speed air): the optimum angle decreases with launch speed and drag coefficient. For a thrown baseball or shot put, optimum is ~42-43 degrees.

With quadratic drag (more realistic at high speed): for a golf ball, optimum is closer to 12-15 degrees (combined with backspin for lift). For an artillery shell, often 30-40 degrees due to high muzzle velocity and dense air.

Why: higher launch angles mean longer flight times, more time exposed to drag, more total energy lost. The trade-off between vertical reach and drag loss shifts the optimum downward.

For a long-jumper, who launches around 7-10 m/s, the optimum angle calculated from biomechanics is ~22 degrees, not 45 — because the long-jumper cannot achieve high vertical velocity from horizontal sprint and because air resistance is minor. Body-mechanics constraints matter more than the equation.

The 45° result is a useful first approximation but should not be taken as universal. Most real-world projectile design uses computational fluid dynamics rather than analytical formulas.
items.why: Textbook results assume ideal conditions. In real applications (golf, baseball, artillery, athletics), the answer is shifted — often substantially — by drag and biomechanical constraints. 'Theoretically 45°' is correct for nothing on Earth.
